$comment: These cases exist ONLY because of binary floating point, and they are shared rather than TypeScript-only because the Kotlin port at AN2 shares the defect and must share the guard (ruling R10). Evaluated naively as 240 * (rate/100) * (7/12), employmentRate 45 yields 63.000000000000007 instead of exactly 63 - and the simplified basis rounds UP, so the error survives rounding and becomes a whole extra day of denominator. A one-day error here moves declarableRate, which is the number filed with the AFC.
rule: totalWorkDays = ceil(simplifiedBasisDays * employmentRate/100 * periodFraction). Multiply before dividing, and normalise before rounding. The normalisation is float hygiene and NOT a regulatory rounding rule.
source: Derived from circular no. 45 of 12 June 2019, point 7.5.1 (the 240-day basis) plus the proration rule. The three cases below were found by scanning employmentRate 1-100 against the period fractions a mid-year start can produce; they are the only ones in that space that diverge.
periodFractionNote: The period is given as an exact ratio, never as a decimal. 7/12 written as 0.5833333333333333 parses to a DIFFERENT double from 7/12 computed, which would make the fixture fail to reproduce the very defect it exists to pin. Both languages must compute the division themselves.

cases.note: The case that motivated the rule. Naive evaluation gives 63.000000000000007, which ceils to 64.
Same shape at a different rate.
Same shape at a different rate.
Control. Full time, full year, no rounding involved - if this ever fails, the basis itself has changed.
Control. 240 * 0.01 = 2.4 rounds UP to 3: a partial day of entitlement is still a working day of denominator.

missionCapNote: PROVISIONAL (ruling R19), an interpretation and not a source. The 10-day mission sub-cap prorates for part-time and partial years, rounded up (SPEC 7.2 step 4). What no source addresses is how it prorates when the employer supplies an EXACT annual total. Interim reading: an exact total is the actual number of days worked and therefore already embodies the working-time rate, so prorating the cap by employmentRate as well would count the same reduction twice and quietly cost a part-timer mission days. Under exact the cap prorates by periodFraction ONLY; under simplified240 by both, because the 240-day basis is a full-time figure not yet reduced. Goes to the reviewer at Checkpoint A. EXACT_METHOD_UNVERIFIED already fires on this path.

missionCapCases.note: Both factors apply: the 240-day basis is full-time and has not been reduced.
PROVISIONAL. The rate is ignored: the 200-day total already embodies it. Before ruling R19 this returned 5.
PROVISIONAL. The period still applies - a mid-year start is a fact about the calendar, not about the rate.
The two readings diverge only for a part-timer, which is why this went unnoticed until the interpretation was written down.

verificationTrace: Ruling R23. Every case carries source_url, verified_by and verified_on. They are EMPTY until the operator fills them at Checkpoint A against the primary source, and a case with empty fields is therefore VISIBLY unverified rather than silently assumed. The tests tolerate the fields and deliberately do NOT require them to be filled: making a green suite depend on verification would create pressure to fill them with something.
